theme: Eyes on the LORD; restored fortunes
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 123 and Psalm 126. Psalm 123 lifts the eyes to God in humble need. Psalm 126 celebrates the return from captivity and then prays for more. Read them together as songs of people who depend completely on God.
settingTheScene: These are two more Songs of Ascents. Psalm 123 is a short, almost whispered prayer of a people who have been treated with contempt. Psalm 126 is a classic song of return: it looks back on the joy of release from exile and forward to the harvest still to come. In the context of this unit, they offer a glimpse of what lies on the far side of the exile.
observation: “To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens!” (123:1).
“Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master… so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us” (123:2).
“Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt” (123:3).
“When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream” (126:1).
“Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy” (126:2).
“The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad” (126:3).
“Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb!” (126:4).
“Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy! He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him” (126:5-6).
interpretation:
Psalm 123 is a prayer of upward gaze. The psalmist lifts his eyes to the one “enthroned in the heavens.” He compares his people to servants who watch their master’s hand, waiting for a signal. The servant does not make demands. He watches, ready, depending on the master for provision. So Israel’s eyes are on the LORD until he shows mercy. The reason is contempt: “We have had more than enough of contempt… the scorn of those who are at ease.” It is the cry of a people who have been mocked and who have only one place to look.

There is humility here that is rare. The servant does not need to understand. He only needs to see the hand. In a world where we are encouraged to look to ourselves, this psalm teaches us to look to God.

Psalm 126 begins with a memory of a joy so great that it seemed like a dream. “When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream.” The return from Babylon was too good to be true. The nations noticed: “The LORD has done great things for them.” And they said so too. Laughter and shouting filled the people.

But then, in verse 4, the psalm becomes a prayer: “Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb.” The Negeb is a dry desert region where streams flow only after the rains, suddenly and abundantly. The people have returned, but the restoration is incomplete. They ask for more. And the psalm ends with a great promise: “Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!” The sower weeps because seed is precious in a famine. Yet he goes out and sows. And he will come home carrying sheaves. The tears are not wasted. Sowing in tears is an act of faith that the harvest will come.

For exiles reading these psalms from afar, they are both a hope and a pattern: depend on God, and remember that sowing in sorrow will end in joy.
connection: Jesus said, “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21), and “Your sorrow will turn into joy” (John 16:20). 2 Corinthians 9:6 says whoever sows bountifully will reap bountifully. Galatians 6:9 says, “Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap.” Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus, for the joy set before him, endured the cross. Revelation 7:17 promises that God will wipe away every tear.
application:
Choose to look to God today as the servant looks to the master’s hand. Wait for his direction.

Think of something you have been “sowing in tears,” such as a hard prayer, a difficult relationship, or a sacrificial act. Continue.

Remember a joy that felt like a dream, and thank God for it.
prayerPrompts: Lift your eyes to God as a servant looks to his master.
Ask him to show mercy to you.
